## Prior stages
## Stage 1 - Ideate

{
  "summary": "Virtualize the real-time waits (`time.sleep`, `time.monotonic`) used in watchdog tests so they become fast, deterministic, and flake-free. The three options range from zero production code change (monkey-patching) to clean interface injection (TimeProvider) to targeted extraction of the timer concern (WatchdogTimer).",
  "options": [
    "Abstract TimeProvider with DI — introduce a TimeProvider protocol/class wrapping sleep/monotonic; production uses RealTimeProvider, tests use VirtualTimeProvider that advances on demand.",
    "Monkey-patch time/threading in test fixtures — use unittest.mock.patch or pytest-mock to replace time.monotonic, time.sleep, etc. with a FakeClock; no production code changes.",
    "Extract a WatchdogTimer class — encapsulate all time operations into a WatchdogTimer that the watchdog delegates to; swap in VirtualWatchdogTimer for tests with an advance() method."
  ]
}

## Stage 2 - Research

{
  "findings": "Production `ActivityWatchdog` already injects `TimeProvider` via its constructor (defaults to `TimeProvider.System`); uses `GetTimestamp()` and `Task.Delay(..., _timeProvider, ct)` — no raw `time.monotonic`/`time.sleep`. Pure decision functions (`DecideOutcome`, `TryDecideSocketWedge`) are already extracted as static methods and tested with simulated time values (synchronous, no real clock). The remaining real-time tests are: (a) `WaitAsync` loop tests that use `Task.Delay`-based pulse pumps and real `Stopwatch` measurements, and (b) integration tests that spawn real child processes via `ProcessCapture.RunAsync` (these involve OS processes and cannot be fully virtualized). No virtual time provider exists yet. A `ManualTimeProvider` must be written or `Microsoft.Extensions.Time.Testing` (providing `FakeTimeProvider`) added as a NuGet dependency. The `Task.Delay` calls in pump helpers are short (<50ms) and carry a real `CancellationToken`, so they already pass the `RealSleepGuard`. The `ActivityWatchdog`'s polling-loop `Task.Delay` (capped at 200ms) already uses the injected `_timeProvider`, so a virtual `TimeProvider.Advance()` would make it return instantly.",
  "constraints": [
    "The `RealSleepGuard` gate (`AllTestProjectCsFiles_AreSleepFree`) bans shell `sleep`, argv-form `(\"sleep\",\"30\")`, and uncancellable `Task.Delay`/`Thread.Sleep` ≥ 1000ms in tests; new code must not introduce real sleeps.",
    "Production `ActivityWatchdog` constructor signature must remain backward-compatible — existing production callers pass no `TimeProvider` and rely on the `TimeProvider.System` default.",
    "Tests that spawn real child processes (`ProcessCapture.RunAsync` with `exec tail -f /dev/null`) exercise real OS process lifecycle and kill signals; those integration tests cannot be fully virtualized — only the watchdog's time dimension can be made fast.",
    "The `ActivityWatchdog` is `internal` and the test project uses `InternalsVisibleTo` — only the test project can access it; a `ManualTimeProvider` helper belongs in the test project.",
    "Pulse pumps (`StartCpuPulsePump`, `StartBurstyWedgePump`, `StartIdleWedgePump`) run as background tasks; a virtual `TimeProvider.Advance()` must coordinate between the pump's `Task.Delay` and the watchdog's polling `Task.Delay` — both use the same `TimeProvider` instance.",
    "`TimeProvider.GetTimestamp()` returns `long` ticks with a `TimestampFrequency`, not raw milliseconds; a virtual provider must return consistent ticks that convert correctly to milliseconds via `TicksToMs`.",
    "The project targets `net10.0`; `System.TimeProvider` is available natively — no external package needed for the base class, but `Microsoft.Extensions.Time.Testing.FakeTimeProvider` (if used) requires adding a NuGet package reference.",
    "The `CliWatchdogTests` (`TimeoutWatchdog`) is a separate tool with its own process-based timeout; it does NOT use `ActivityWatchdog` or `TimeProvider` and is out of scope for this task."
  ]
}

{
  "evidence": "The `ActivityWatchdog` already injects `TimeProvider?` via its constructor (ProcessRunners.Watchdog.cs:78, defaults to `TimeProvider.System` at line 85). Its polling loop uses `Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(delay), _timeProvider, ct)` at line 284 — the overload that accepts a `TimeProvider`. Pure decision functions `DecideOutcome` (line 162) and `TryDecideSocketWedge` (line 143) are already static and tested synchronously with simulated time values. No `ManualTimeProvider`, `FakeTimeProvider`, or `Microsoft.Extensions.Time.Testing` package exists in the codebase (confirmed by grep across all .cs and .csproj files and `find` on disk).

Four test methods still run the real `WaitAsync` polling loop against real wall-clock time, each creating `ActivityWatchdog` with the default `TimeProvider.System`:

1. `ActivityWatchdogSocketWedgeTests.WaitAsync_CpuPulseMasksDeadline_SocketWedgeStillFires` (line 79–116): Creates watchdog with `inactivityTimeoutMs=1_500`, runs `StartCpuPulsePump` (a background `Task.Run` loop calling `Task.Delay(50, stop)` and `watchdog.Pulse("cpu")`), then calls `await watchdog.WaitAsync(CancellationToken.None)` and measures elapsed with `Stopwatch`. Asserts `sw.ElapsedMilliseconds < inactivityMs + 3_000`. Total real wait: ~1.5 s.

2. `ActivityWatchdogSocketWedgeTests.WaitAsync_BusySubtree_NotKilled_EvenWithSocketAndSilence` (line 126–151): Same pattern with `inactivityMs=800` and `stopCts = new CancellationTokenSource(inactivityMs * 4)`. Total real wait: ~3.2 s.

3. `ActivityWatchdogSocketWedgeTests.SustainedIdle.WaitAsync_BurstyAgent_IdleSampleButRecentCpuBurst_NotKilled` (line 64–88): Runs both `StartCpuPulsePump` and `StartBurstyWedgePump` (which calls `Task.Delay(windowMs / 8, stop)` inside a loop). Observes for `inactivityMs * 5` via `CancellationTokenSource`. Total real wait: ~5 s.

4. `ActivityWatchdogSocketWedgeTests.SustainedIdle.WaitAsync_SustainedIdlePlusSocket_StillFiresSocketWedge` (line 98–127): `inactivityMs=1_200`, runs both pumps. Total real wait: ~1.2 s.

5. `SwivalSubagentRunnerWatchdogTests.ActivityWatchdog.WaitAsync_BurstThenTotalSilence_FiresAtInactivityDeadline` (line 140–174): Contains `await Task.Delay(50)` at line 155 WITHOUT a `CancellationToken` (the only uncancellable `Task.Delay` in watchdog tests, though at 50 ms it's under the RealSleepGuard's 1000 ms threshold). Then waits ~2 s for the watchdog loop. Total real wait: ~2 s.

The pump helpers (`StartCpuPulsePump`, `StartBurstyWedgePump`, `StartIdleWedgePump`) all use `Task.Delay(int, CancellationToken)` — the overload that does NOT accept a `TimeProvider`. To virtualize, these pumps must switch to `Task.Delay(TimeSpan, TimeProvider, CancellationToken)` and receive the same `ManualTimeProvider` instance as the watchdog. The watchdog's own `WaitAsync` already uses the `TimeProvider`-aware `Task.Delay` overload (line 284), so virtualizing it requires only injecting a `ManualTimeProvider`.

The `Stopwatch` assertions (e.g., `sw.ElapsedMilliseconds < inactivityMs + 3_000`) measure real wall-clock time and will report ~0 ms when time is virtualized; they must be replaced with assertions on the watchdog's reported `SilenceMs`/`SubtreeIdleForMs` or virtual-clock derived values.

Integration tests that spawn real child processes via `ProcessCapture.RunAsync` or `SwivalSubagentRunner.RunAsync` (e.g., `RunAsync_TotallySilentProcess_KilledAtFirstOutputDeadline`, `RunAsync_SilentThenActive_KilledNoResurrection`, `RunAsync_EarlyBurstThenTotalSilence_KilledAtInactivityDeadline`) involve real OS processes and `ProcessCapture`'s own `SampleTreeCpuLoopAsync` (ProcessCapture.cs:221) which also uses `Task.Delay(intervalMs, ct)` without a `TimeProvider`. These cannot be fully virtualized — only the watchdog's time dimension can be made fast.

The `RealSleepGuard` gate (`AllTestProjectCsFiles_AreSleepFree`) is currently passing (line 149 is `[Fact]`, not `[Fact(Skip)]`) — the existing tests comply because all `Task.Delay` calls either carry a real `CancellationToken` or are under 1000 ms. A `ManualTimeProvider` must not introduce any new real sleeps.",
